prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and the microfounded analysis of monetary policy.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B012 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. Round 1 left no configuration with six explicit supporters, so I tested whether my first choice survives the chair's questions. I think it does, but with less margin than I first stated. The chair asked whether the discovery is the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms or the usable policy framework. I take the discovery to be origination. Calvo's staggered pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's microfounded policy analysis are separable and identifiable. That reading is why I do not widen the trio to the estimation and quantitative strand (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets, Gertler). That strand is a distinct achievement and does not fit within three names. On the 2008 and 2021-23 episodes, I have seen nothing in the exchange that shows the core mechanisms were refuted. The evidence shows the framework was modified, and the shift toward heterogeneous-agent and financial-friction extensions builds on it. Four decades of use, critique and revision is the kind of confirmation I weigh most heavily. On Taylor, I accept the point made by Hassler, Friberg and Teorell that the rule alone would be thin. My case for him rests on the staggered-contracts model, with the rule as the part that connected theory to policy practice. I would accept Gali in place of Taylor if the Committee prefers it, since the choice is a judgement about origination versus integrated evaluation. What changed is my alternatives. I drop B001 and add B007. The robustness and measurement concerns raised by Dreber-Almenberg, Hassler, Krusell and Strömberg, together with the four-author credit and Vishny's omission, weigh more heavily on B001 than I allowed in round 1. Boppart's argument that Kiyotaki-Moore is a different mechanism from the 2022 bank-run prize, with a clean two-author attribution, is persuasive enough to lift B007 above B001. I keep B026 as my first alternative. I do not treat support counts as merit.
statement.case_against: The credit is still diffuse, and that is the strongest argument against my own choice. Any three-name cut omits Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets or Gertler, whose work made the framework operational. B026 and B007 have cleaner attribution (two names each), and I should not dismiss that. Friberg's point about state-dependent price adjustment is a real scientific qualification of Calvo's time-dependent assumption. The framework's record in 2008 and 2021-23 is contested, and the field is moving toward heterogeneous-agent models. A prize built on originators honours the conceptual core more than the empirical and implementation work that gave the framework its reach. I have not independently verified the literature behind these points.

responses.point: Friberg supports the same Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio but raises a specific scientific reservation. Micro evidence on price adjustment, including asymmetric adjustment, points to state-dependent behaviour closer to menu-cost models than to Calvo's time-dependent mechanism. He would not object to substituting Gali.
responses.response: I take this as the most serious scientific qualification inside our shared configuration, and the chair's question about it is fair. My view is that it bears on how well the mechanism describes micro price data and does not remove Calvo's role in originating the staggered-pricing device from which the New Keynesian Phillips curve was built. A tractable approximation that organised decades of research and was then challenged by micro evidence is a normal path for a foundational contribution. The citation should say what Calvo did, which is staggered price setting, and should not claim that time-dependent adjustment is the empirically correct description. I do not think Gali is a better answer to your concern, because his canonical model uses the same Calvo pricing. I accept the Gali substitution for Taylor, not for Calvo, and only if the Committee weighs integrated evaluation over origination.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 only as an alternative. He argues that eight credited names make any three-person cut hard to defend, and he proposes a two-part prize combining Kiyotaki-Moore with Melitz alone, while admitting that a one-person B026 part may look like a product of the cap.
responses.response: I accept the attribution objection and have not removed it. I still think diffuse later credit does not undercut the importance of the originating contributions. I would answer it by writing a citation about nominal rigidities and the microfounded analysis of policy, not the whole framework. On the two-part proposal, I would not support it as a way to bridge differences. Joining B007 and B026 mixes two unrelated discoveries, and Melitz alone is a part the cap forces and not one anyone prefers on merit. If the Committee goes to B026 or B007, I would rather see each as a clean standalone prize than a combination built to collect votes. That is a view about the discoveries and not about counting support.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B007 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the collateral mechanism is a clean two-author discovery, distinct from the 2022 bank-run prize because it is a dynamic general-equilibrium feedback with no bank failure required. He ranked B012 fourth because of attribution, and he accepts that empirical identification of collateral channels is weaker than the theory.
responses.response: Your distinction from the 2022 prize is persuasive and has moved me. I now treat B007 as a real alternative where I ranked it sixth at opening. Your reply to Krusell also helps, since the pair avoids adding Gertler and re-opening the accelerator overlap with Bernanke. Where we still differ is scope. Nominal rigidity underlies how a whole policy field is modelled, while collateral amplification is a narrower mechanism. In my judgement that outweighs the cleaner attribution, but I accept that the weighting is contestable, and I would not call B007 a weak choice. I would not call the identification concern decisive. It applies to many macro mechanisms, including parts of mine.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B026 with Melitz and Helpman. She argues that the heterogeneous-firm framework is a distinct advance from the 2008 prize, is validated by firm-level data, and has compact and tractable credit. She leaves out Redding as more derivative.
responses.response: Hjalmarsson's case is the strongest challenge to my ordering, because B026 has the cleaner credit and the more direct empirical confirmation. I find her distinction from the 2008 prize convincing. I also accept that the 'derivative' judgement on Redding is an attribution call that the Committee should state openly. What keeps me on B012 is the open attribution question she acknowledges: the uncredited Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum strand, and the question of why Helpman is the second name. I do not claim B012's attribution is cleaner. I claim its three originators are more separable and its scope is wider. If the Committee settles those B026 questions and weights attribution and repeated empirical testing above breadth, B026 would be an entirely defensible first choice for me.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the discovery as origination (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or as the usable policy framework, in which case Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler would weigh more.
How far the micro evidence on state-dependent price adjustment weakens the Calvo contribution, as opposed to refining it.
How heavily to weigh the framework's record after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation against its conceptual and policy influence.
Whether breadth of influence (B012) should outweigh cleaner two-name attribution and more direct empirical confirmation (B026, B007).

Whether the B026 questions about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum and about Helpman as second name can be settled in favour of a Melitz-Helpman pair. I have not independently verified citation or priority details.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman is apparent from my supplied profile. My research field is market and mechanism design, which is not a field of any preferred or alternative candidate. I disclose my SSE affiliation alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. Friberg supports the same trio and I respond to him above, but I do not treat these connections as a conflict with any candidate. I also disclose my role as an editor at the Scandinavian Journal of Economics and at Games and Economic Behavior. None of these ties is adjudicated.
